10888-arthur-hamilton-and-his-dog:
Arthur Hamilton and His Dog, written for the Massachusetts Sabbath School Society and approved in 1851, is a Sunday school tale of a boy and his pet. One October evening Arthur plays before his family's small brown cottage with his brother James and a large spotted dog. Rover bows on his hind legs, tosses bread off his nose, begs with imploring paws, and barks his thanks.

The story follows Arthur leaving home, with Rover as companion and moral teacher. Its lessons are gentle: kindness, obedience, and faith in daily life. Children get a simple, affectionate tale, in the earnest style of mid-century Sunday books.
14375-the-adventures-of-grandfather-frog:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote this 1920 bedtime book about Grandfather Frog of the Smiling Pool, with pictures by Harrison Cady. The old frog, proud of his big mouth and fine voice, keeps getting into scrapes.

Longlegs the heron hunts him, Billy Mink and Little Joe Otter stir up trouble, and Spotty the turtle comes to his rescue more than once. Each short chapter ends with a gentle lesson on patience, vanity, or care. The pond setting returns in Burgess's later animal books. Burgess fills the pond with animal neighbors, and the book remains a mild, charming read for young children.
22750-rags-the-story-of-a-dog:
Karen Niemann wrote Rags: The Story of a Dog, a children's story told around a little boy, his grandmother, and the dog of the title. The catalog record gives no year. Animal stories for the young were a staple of the era, teaching kindness through a pet's fortunes.

The sample finds Gary building a playhouse from boxes of his own. Once the wood is carried in and the walks are swept, he calls out that everything is done. Then he asks his grandmother if he may play in the box house now. Chores first, then play, is the story's gentle economy, with Rags at the center of the household's affections. The book offers young readers a warm, simple tale of a dog and the family that loves him.
22842-the-widow-s-dog:
An American visitor meets an English flower in The Widow's Dog, a sketch by Mary Russell Mitford. The narrator recalls a favorite moment with real pleasure. She showed a visiting American the humble harebell growing wild, right where her sketch is set. He had never seen the wildflower, though poetry had consecrated it in their shared language.

He placed it in his buttonhole and quoted Scott's Lady of the Lake with enthusiasm. Around that small scene, Mitford builds her tale of a widow and the dog at its center. Flowers, loyalty, and village memory intertwine in her usual manner. The piece shows her gift for finding a whole story inside an afternoon's walk and a stranger's delight.
2393-his-dog:
Albert Payson Terhune's His Dog gathers more Sunnybank stories, this time centering on the bond between a man and his dog. The tales show dogs as workers, friends, and family, facing danger with unshowy courage. Terhune writes from his life as a breeder, and the kennel details ring true.

The collection's sentiment is sincere rather than cloying, and its best stories still touch readers. Dog lovers will find a gentle, nostalgic book. It complements the Lad and Bruce volumes. Terhune wrote for dog magazines as well as for book readers.
2735-the-golden-dog:
William Kirby wrote this Canadian romance, Le Chien d'Or, first published in the United States in 1877 without his knowledge or sanction. Kirby's prefatory note protests that weak copyright laws left him powerless to stop that edition, and this text restores his work.

The Golden Dog follows old Quebec under French rule, with merchants, soldiers, and lovers caught in rivalry and revenge. Kirby writes with local pride and historical color. The novel endures as a classic of Canadian literature, and a tale of a city built on trade and pride. Kirby's Quebec feels lived in, from market to council chamber.
308-three-men-in-a-boat-to-say-nothing-o:
Jerome K. Jerome claims his book's chief beauty is simple truthfulness, not style or knowledge. Three Men in a Boat, published in 1889, records a Thames boating holiday by Jerome, George, Harris, and the dog Montmorency. The preface insists the men are flesh and blood.

George weighs about twelve stone, the preface notes, and the adventures really happened, only colored a little. River mishaps, camping quarrels, and Hampton Court history fill the trip. Jerome's comic asides made the book a lasting bestseller. It remains the classic Thames holiday tale. Jerome's Thames comedy has never gone out of print since 1889.
4506-lost-in-the-fog:
James De Mille wrote this boys' adventure in 1870, opening on a beautiful July morning at Grand Pre. A crowd of boys gathers on the wharf, where the tide is high and the turbid waters of Mud Creek run. Old acquaintances gather round old scenes, with a roundabout plan for a roundabout voyage, while the doctor warns and remonstrates in vain.

The voyage must be done, and the boys set out into fog, tide, and mishap. De Mille writes with humor about Nova Scotia boys, boats, and blunders. Lost in the Fog suits young readers who enjoy sailing yarns, where a simple trip turns eventful and the fog does its worst.
5759-the-day-of-the-dog:
George Barr McCutcheon published The Day of the Dog in New York in 1904, with illustrations by Harrison Fisher. Part one opens with Crosby planning a hurried train trip, since he has heard Mrs Delancy leaves for New York that night, and delay would bring troublesome complications. Crosby promises Graves he will join a box party that evening, then faces three hours of rank scenery each way, plus a drive into the country.

It offers a light society comedy of appointments, trains, and tangled plans, told with McCutcheon's polished ease. The novel favors witty talk and social maneuver over grand drama, as a single day's errands threaten a whole evening's pleasures. Fans of early twentieth-century popular romance will enjoy its brisk pace and its picture of fashionable life on the move.
5947-billy-bunny-and-uncle-bull-frog:
David Cory tells linked bedtime stories of Billy Bunny and Uncle Bull Frog, in a series that also includes Billy Bunny and Daddy Fox, the Friendly Elephant, and Uncle Lucky Lefthindfoot. Illustrations by Hugh Spencer accompany the tales, which proceed story by story, each ending with a promise of what comes next. One story finds the Policeman Cat arresting Billy Bunny and Uncle Lucky, raising his club to tickle a hind foot.

A big elm tree begins to bark just then, scaring the Policeman Cat nearly to death, since he mistakes it for a dog. Young readers get gentle woodland comedy, where rabbits, frogs, cats, and trees play at danger without real harm. The book suits bedtime reading aloud, with short stories, familiar animal friends, and a storyteller's voice that pauses for tomorrow.
7281-tom-cringle-s-log:
Michael Scott's Tom Cringle's Log opens with Thomas Cringle, thirteen years old and four feet four inches, dazzled by the glories of Trafalgar in a merry month of May. He resolves that Britain shall no longer languish for want of a successor to Nelson. He sets himself to torment every man and woman connected with him until they agree to exert all their influence for his naval career.

The boy's grand resolve, told in his own comic voice, launches a sea tale of ships, storms, and West Indian life. Scott writes with a sailor's gusto and a humourist's eye for youthful swagger. Cringle's log follows a small hero with large dreams onto a very large ocean.
7884-in-the-fog:
Richard Harding Davis's In the Fog opens at the Grill, called the hardest club in the world to enter. Membership there rivals a Garter or a Vanity Fair cartoon. Members never name it, lest praise sound like boasting, and they still blot letters with sand.

The club dates to Shakespeare's Theatre on the Times site. It holds a golden grill from Charles II and Pierce Egan's Tom and Jerry manuscript, and has blackballed a prime minister of each party at one sitting. Through fog, supper talk, and four strangers, Davis builds a witty London mystery.
9463-the-under-dog:
F. Hopkinson Smith wrote this book of the under dog in 1903, illustrated throughout. His preface defines the term: men who lose place through weakness, lost chances, or impaired powers, and must always be under dog in the fight. Others are misjudged by fellows, or crushed by law with a sentence, while still others are misunderstood and out of touch.

Such men, Smith says, have hearts chilled by neglect, whose coals need only a warm breath of sympathy to flame again. His tales follow such figures with compassion. The book remains a humane collection, Victorian in sentiment and generous in spirit.
9478-the-dog:
William Youatt wrote The Dog in the mid-1800s, a full guide to dogs for owners, breeders, and vets of the day. E. J. Lewis, a Philadelphia doctor, edited this edition and added new matter. The book covers breeds from bloodhounds and greyhounds to spaniels, terriers, and sheep dogs, with plates of each type. It treats the dog as a working friend, not a mere pet.

Pages take up form, temper, training, kennel care, and ills of each breed, from the Newfoundland to the tiny Blenheim. Youatt draws on long practice with hounds and gun dogs, and gives plain rules for feed, work, and cure. A reader gets a rich picture of Victorian dog life, and a store of old lore on breeds that still walk our streets today.
billy-bunny-and-uncle-bull-frog: David Cory's 1920 children's book collects short tales of Billy Bunny and his animal neighbours. Billy meets Mr. Blacksnake, a freshwater crab, a sorrowful jay bird, a policeman cat, a gray mouse and Uncle Bull Frog, and tries novelties like the ting-a-ling telephone. Each brief adventure ends kindly, in the vein of Cory's other Billy Bunny volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gog-and-magog:
Gog and Magog are the names, respectively, of a king and his supposed kingdom, named several times in Ezekiel 38 and 39, and a single time in the Apocalypse. Ezekiel is commanded to set his face against Gog, the land of Magog, chief prince of Mosoch and Thubal. A Catholic Encyclopedia article weighs the vague evidence for who and where they were.

Gog's invasion host includes Persians, Ethiopians, Libyans, Gomer, and the house of Thogorma. It comes from the northern parts. Some writers read Gog as a generic figure for the enemies of Israel, or of the Church, and others as a royal title like Pharaoh. More probably both names are historical: Gog may be Gyges of Lydia, called Gu-gu on Assyrian inscriptions, though Josephus and others identify Magog with Scythia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-baptis:
Johann Baptist Alzog, a Catholic church historian born at Ohlau in 1808 and dead at Freiburg in 1878. He studied at Breslau and Bonn, was ordained in 1834, and took a Munich doctorate in 1835. After Posen in 1836, Hildesheim in 1845, he took Freiburg's church history chair in 1853 with a councillor's rank.

Alzog stoutly defended Posen's Archbishop Dunin against Prussian persecution, and later joined the Vatican preparatory commission on dogma. Amiable and virtuous in character, he wrote a Manual of Church History through nine editions to 1872 in many tongues, a Patrology through four editions. There is also an edition of Gregory Nazianzen's Apologetic Oration, besides wide periodical work.
doe-osti-17014396-firetec-bug-resolution: A wildfire simulator's growing pains got their diary, and this DOE log records FIRETEC's bug resolutions. Developers see what broke and how it was fixed. The code's history stays honest. The log was maintained. The diary was honest. The code was FIRETEC's.
doe-osti-2571040-evonet-a-phylogenomic-a: EvoNet's plant survival genes got their DOE report, and this text covers the phylogenomic systems biology approach. The pages detail the gene hunt. The botanists get their candidates. The plants were marginal, low-nitrogen. The hunt was gene. The approach was systems biology.
doe-osti-2571553-interactions-between-ae: Dust and baby clouds danced over Argentina, and this DOE final report tracks the CACTI field campaign. The pages detail the aerosol-cloud tango. The cloud physicists get their data. The data were hard-won. The campaign was CACTI. The tango was aerosol-cloud.
doe-osti-2999893-the-ai-base-nda-catalog: The AI-Base NDA catalog got its DOE text, and this report lists the data assets. The pages detail the catalog. The AI teams get their reference. The catalog was AI-Base NDA. The reference was data assets. The reference was AI.
doe-osti-3003183-packages-of-distributed: Distributed energy packages got demonstrated, and this DOE text covers community demand flexibility. The pages detail the findings. The grid folks get their playbook. The scale was community. The playbook was grid. The flexibility was demand. The scale was grid.
doe-osti-3014667-security-of-ders-and-gr: DER security got slid, and this DOE deck covers grid edge technologies. The pages detail the findings. The security folks get their briefing. The format was slides. The briefing was security. The technologies were edge. The deck was DOE's. The security was DERs.
doe-osti-3018361-advanced-mixed-mode-com: Hydrogen combustors got mixed-mode-advanced, and this DOE final retrofits F-class. The pages detail the report findings. The energy folks get their closeout. The retrofit was F-class. The closeout was energy. The class was F. The mode was mixed.
doe-osti-3019695-development-of-pnnl-s-p: PNNL got plutonium-metallographied, and this DOE text develops the capability. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The lab was PNNL. The data were nuclear. The capability was metallography. The PNNL was development. The plutonium was capability.
doe-osti-3021668-grid-resiliency-using-h: Wildfires got hydro-microgridded, and this DOE text builds grid resiliency. The pages detail the findings. The grid folks get their data. The microgrids were hydro-based. The data were grid. The wildfires were resiliency. The based were hydro. The microgrids were DOE.
his-dog:
Albert Payson Terhune gave his 1922 novel His Dog a hero ground down by dirt farming in the North Jersey hills. Link Ferris inherited forty worked-out acres, a mortgage, and a shack from his Civil War veteran father, and his life runs in a circle of labor, sleep, and hard cider. Into that barren routine comes a dog, and the four long chapters, The Derelict, The Battle, The Ordeal, and The Choice, turn on what the animal asks of him.

Terhune's derelict is the man, not the dog: the collie's devotion becomes the one claim on Link that the farm cannot make. The story is spare beside the Sunnybank books, a redemption tale in which a dog's faithfulness rebuilds a wasted life.
lost-in-the-fog:
Lost in the Fog is a sea adventure for boys by James De Mille, dated 1870. It opens on a July morning on the wharf of Grand Pré. A crowd of schoolboys gathers there, old friends with names like Bruce, Arthur, Bart, and Tom. They are bound on a voyage aboard the Antelope, against the Doctor's warnings.

The boys are old acquaintances from Grand Pré School, and they talk like seasoned sailors. Their roundabout plan sets them on a highly eventful voyage. Fog, sea risk, and boyish daring drive the tale from the first chapter. De Mille writes with humor and a love of the Nova Scotia coast. It is a lively period piece of schoolboy adventure at sea.
navajo-weavers-third-annual-report-of-th:
Washington Matthews wrote Navajo Weavers for the third annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology, covering 1881 to 1882. The Government Printing Office issued it in Washington in 1884. Matthews served as a United States Army doctor. Plates show a woman spinning, a blanket loom, and belt weaving.

Figures lay out how warp threads run, how healds are set, and how saddle girths are woven. Other plates show finished blankets, some of the finest quality. Matthews also shows Zuni women weaving a belt for contrast. The piece records tools and steps in detail, so later readers can follow exactly how Navajo cloth was made.
our-friend-the-dog:
Maurice Maeterlinck, the Belgian author of The Life of the Bee, wrote Our Friend the Dog. The essay begins in grief. He has just lost Pelléas, a little bulldog of six months. The pup's knowing eyes opened to love mankind. They closed again on the cruel secrets of death. The name, he muses, could disgrace no man or hero. How can a poor dog be anything but loving, devoted, and faithful?

Pelléas had a bulging, powerful forehead, like Socrates or Verlaine. He had a smile Maeterlinck starts to describe. Then the essay turns from portrait to philosophy. In Alexander Teixeira de Mattos's translation it became a famous tribute. It asks what humans owe the one animal that chose them.
podcast-joerogan--s2d7cojsog:
Neuroscientist Andrew Huberman joins Joe Rogan for episode 1683 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Huberman is a Stanford professor whose own show made health steps a mass craze. His talks with Rogan are among the show's most saved.

Huberman lays out steps for sleep, light, focus, and strength that rest on lab work. He tells what he does at dawn, at work, and at night to keep his mind keen. Rogan tests the steps against his own hard routine. Listeners get a dense, useful talk. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated methods.
podcast-joerogan-zvqTC4nQkog:
Chef and TV star Matty Matheson tells Joe Rogan about growing up Mormon and being excommunicated in this clip. Matheson, known for loud humor and hit cooking shows, had a wild road from a strict faith to food fame. The story mixes church, family, and rebellion.

Matheson describes the rules and community of his Mormon youth with warmth and bite. He explains the break that led the church to cast him out and the rough years that followed. Rogan draws out the funny and painful parts in equal measure. Hungry and curious listeners get a meaty tale of faith lost and a life rebuilt.
the-adventures-of-grandfather-frog: For his Bedtime Story-Books, Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Grandfather Frog. Harrison Cady drew the plates. Little, Brown, and Company printed it at Boston in 1920. Chapters listed bring Billy Mink to the Smiling Pool first. Little Joe Otter joins him there. Longlegs the Blue Heron then pays a set of calls. Grandfather Frog's big mouth lands him in trouble. Spotty the Turtle plays doctor at the end.
the-camp-of-the-dog:
Algernon Blackwood opens The Camp of the Dog, dated 1908, with a voyage among islands. Past Stockholm the islands run north in their hundreds, of every shape and size. The little steamer that threads their intricate mazes in summer leaves the traveller bewildered as to the points of the compass by the time it reaches Waxholm. The tale is set in five parts, named by number alone.

After Waxholm, the narrator says, the true islands begin to run wild, up the coast in a tangled hundred-mile course of empty beauty. In the very heart of that confusion the party pitched their tents for a summer holiday. A wilderness of islands lay about them. Some lay so close that a strip of water no wider than a country lane ran between them.
the-day-of-the-dog: George Barr McCutcheon's The Day of the Dog was printed in New York in 1904, with pictures by Harrison Fisher and decorations by Margaret and Helen Maitland Armstrong. It is shown here only through its long list of illustrations. The captions name a dog called Swallow, a Mr. Crosby, Mrs. Delancy, Mrs. Austin, and Mr. Higgins, with scenes at a big red barn, a shallow brook, a theatre, and a place called Lonesomeville. Only the front matter and picture list are present here, so the tale itself does not appear.
the-dog:
William Youatt's The Dog, edited with added notes by E. J. Lewis, is dated 1852 and was first entered in 1846. A list of plates names breed after breed. It runs from the southern hound and bloodhound to the Thibet dog and the dingo. It ends with the greyhound, the water spaniel, the poodle, and the Newfoundland. The English and Scotch sheep dogs close the roll.

Youatt was the age's chief voice on animal health. His book joins breed lore with care, training, and disease cures. Lewis, a Philadelphia doctor, adds notes for American readers. It stays a rich source on how the 1800s knew their dogs.
the-golden-dog:
William Kirby wrote The Golden Dog. It is also given as Le Chien d'Or. His prefatory note is signed at Niagara, Canada, in May 1897. The note tells the history of the book. A first edition came out in the United States in 1877. It came out without his knowledge. Weak copyright law let it go on selling in many editions. All profited but the author.

Kirby says L. C. Page and Company of Boston then stepped in. They asked him to revise the book. This revised edition is the only one with his sanction. He corrected it by the latest findings on the history of Quebec. The contents open with Men of the Old Regime. They name The Walls of Quebec and A Chatelaine of New France. They also name The Intendant Bigot. The tale is set in French Quebec under the old regime.
the-great-red-frog:
M. Yendis told and pictured The Great Red Frog. Methuen and Company printed it in London in 1903. Long ago, in a land far off, there lived a little Prince who looked just like the Lord Chamberlain's son. The likeness fooled even the sly old Chamberlain, who at times could not say which boy was which. The two grew up as playmates.

In time the Prince came to rule as King of Noware, and the pair still matched like two peas. One day, at play outdoors, a strange thing happened: a Magic Bush sprang up at the King's back. In that moment the Chamberlain's son lost his temper and shoved the King into the bush. The King came out a queer red Frog, and off it hopped, croaking in fright. The tale is a picture-book story for children. It is told page by page with the pictures.
the-under-dog:
F. Hopkinson Smith gathered his stories of life's losers in The Under Dog, published in 1903. A letter to readers opens the volume and sorts these figures into kinds. Some lose place through weakness or missed chances, some are misjudged by neighbours or crushed by the law, and some simply need sympathy to revive.

Smith says such people, grave and gay, have always appealed to him, and he prints their stories hoping readers will feel the same. The contents begin with a group called No Respecter of Persons. Its pieces include The Crime of Samanthy North, Bud Tilden the mail-thief, and a sentence measured out as eleven months and ten days.
the-voice-in-the-fog:
Harold MacGrath published The Voice in the Fog in 1915 with Grosset and Dunlap and the Bobbs-Merrill Company, illustrated by A. B. Wenzell. He dedicates the novel to Cav. Giovanni Piccinini, remembering happy Florentine days. A frontispiece names a character, Kitty Killigrew, before the story starts.

Chapter one is a single subject: fog. MacGrath renders a London fog as solid and substantial, yellow as an old dog's tooth or a jaundiced eye. Sight fails completely inside it, and only touch stays trustworthy, feeling the vapour's substance on the palms and through clothing. The opening withholds people and plot, letting weather itself become the mystery's first actor.
three-men-in-a-boat-to-say-nothing-of-th:
Jerome K. Jerome published Three Men in a Boat, to say nothing of the dog, at Bristol and London in 1889, with illustrations by A. Frederics. His preface claims the book's chief beauty is simple truthfulness. Its pages record events that really happened, only coloured a little at no extra charge.

George, Harris, and Montmorency are flesh and blood, he insists, especially George at about twelve stone. Other books may beat it in depth or originality, Jerome says, but none in incurable veracity. Readers get a Thames boating holiday turned into enduring comic travel writing.
tom-cringle-s-log:
Michael Scott, who lived from 1789 to 1835, narrates his naval log through Thomas Cringle, a boy dazzled by Trafalgar's glories. Cringle stands four feet four inches tall at thirteen and resolves that Britain needs a successor to Nelson. He torments every relative until their influence converges on an admiral.

A letter with a formidable seal then arrives at Sunday breakfast, and his mother weeps over it in silence. She pushes the manuscript toward him, covers her face, and leaves the room praying. Readers get a comic, sorrowful start to a sailor's career, launched by a child's ambition.
